Both answers hit the key points: change the axis, reframe breadth as cost, timed task-based evals, land beside the incumbent, and qualify out bad-fit deals. Neither contains a factual error.

A adds things that would change what the asker does next. It says to build the must-haves (SSO, audit logs, SOC 2) because positioning can't fix them. It separates a roadmap problem from a positioning problem. It recommends interviewing lost and won deals to find the wedge. It also says to pick a narrow wedge and name who you're not for. These make it more complete and more honest about when judo doesn't work. It also gets in before the RFP and renames the category, which covers "reframe early in the sale" well.

B is punchier. It has good tactical ideas: demo "landmines" and architecture the incumbent can't retrofit. It also tells the asker to walk away from procurement-owned rubrics, which matches "if you're in their bake-off on their terms, you already lost." But it lacks the segment and wedge focus, the diagnostic step, and the must-haves caveat. The trap questions are somewhat aggressive.

A is more decision-relevant overall because of the diagnostic and the table-stakes caveat. B is stronger on disqualifying buyers and on its architectural angle. A is somewhat better.
